fact: In February 2016, EPA and CDC/ATSDR, working with the Consumer Product Safety Commission, launched a multi-agency research effort, the Federal Research Action Plan, on recycled tire rubber used as infill on playing fields.
quote: To help address concerns raised by the public about potential exposures and health effects due to the use of recycled tire rubber used on fields as infill material, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, in collaboration with the Consumer Product Safety Commission, launched a multi-agency research effort in February 2016 called the Federal Research Action Plan on the Use of Tire Crumbs in Playing Fields.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Federal Research on Recycled Tire Crumb Used on Playing Fields and Playgrounds (last updated July 8, 2026)

fact: EPA and CDC/ATSDR released their findings in two parts: Part 1 in 2019 on what is in tire crumb rubber, and Part 2 in April 2024 on how people using synthetic turf fields may be exposed to its chemicals.
quote: EPA and CDC/ATSDR reported research findings in two parts. Part 1, which was released in 2019, communicated the research objectives, methods, results and findings for the tire crumb rubber characterization research (i.e., what is in the material). Part 2, which was released in April 2024, includes data to characterize potential human exposures to the chemicals found in the tire crumb rubber material while using synthetic turf fields.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Federal Research on Recycled Tire Crumb Used on Playing Fields and Playgrounds (last updated July 8, 2026)

fact: EPA calls the federal effort the largest tire crumb rubber study done in the United States and says its reports, taken together, are not a risk assessment.
quote: Based upon available literature, this research effort represents the largest tire crumb rubber study conducted in the United States. While these reports together are not a risk assessment, the information and results from the effort will fill specific data gaps about the potential for human exposure to chemical constituents associated with tire crumb rubber used in synthetic turf fields.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Federal Research on Recycled Tire Crumb Used on Playing Fields and Playgrounds (last updated July 8, 2026)

fact: EPA and ATSDR concluded that chemicals are present in tire crumb and exposures can occur but are likely limited: little of most organic chemicals reaches the air, under 1 to 3% of the metals dissolve in simulated body fluids, players' blood metals matched the general population, and urine PAH markers did not differ between turf and grass players.
quote: In general, the findings from the entire playing fields field portion of the FRAP study (both the Tire Crumb Characterization Part 1 and the Tire Crumb Exposure Characterization Part 2 combined) support the conclusion that although chemicals are present (as expected) in the tire crumb rubber and exposures can occur, they are likely limited, for example: Generally, only small amounts of most organic chemicals are released from tire crumb into the air through emissions. … For metals, only small fractions (i.e., <1 to 3%) are released from tire crumb rubber into simulated biological fluids compared to a default assumption of 100% bioaccessibility. In the biomonitoring pilot study, concentrations for metals measured in blood were similar to those in the general population. No differences in PAH metabolites in urine were observed between study participants using synthetic turf fields compared to those using grass fields.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Federal Research on Recycled Tire Crumb Used on Playing Fields and Playgrounds (last updated July 8, 2026)

fact: The federal exposure report says tire crumb rubber, sometimes mixed with sand, is added to sports turf for ballast, to support the blades and to cushion players, and counts 18,000 to 19,000 synthetic turf fields in the United States with 1,200 to 1,500 new installations a year, about half of them replacements.
quote: These third-generation systems typically use small pieces of recycled tires, referred to as “recycled tire crumb rubber” (or simply “tire crumb rubber”), to fill the space between the polyethylene yarn fibers. The recycled tire crumb rubber (sometimes mixed with sand or other raw materials) is added for ballast, support for the synthetic grass blades, and as cushioning for field users. … There are between 18,000 and 19,000 synthetic turf fields in the United States, with 1,200 – 1,500 new installations each year, about half of which are replacements.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Synthetic Turf Field Recycled Tire Crumb Rubber Research Under the Federal Research Action Plan, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary
notes: The field counts are the report's footnote 2, a personal communication with the Synthetic Turf Council; say so if the count is used as more than scale.

fact: The federal exposure report says artificial turf at homes does not typically include tire crumb rubber, so residential turf was not part of the study.
quote: While artificial turf is also used at residences, that turf does not typically include tire crumb rubber; as a result, the use of artificial turf at residences is not part of the FRAP study.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary, footnote 3

fact: The federal reports found emissions of most tested chemicals from tire crumb were low at 25 °C (77°F) but higher for some at 60 °C (140°F), and that exposures may be higher on indoor fields than outdoor ones.
quote: Emissions of most SVOCs and many VOCs were low when tested at 25 °C, while emissions were higher for some, but not all at 60 °C. … Exposures may be higher for people using indoor synthetic turf fields than outdoor fields.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary
notes: The Fahrenheit figures are conversions (25 °C = 77°F, 60 °C = 140°F), not the report's.

fact: The federal pilot sampled 25 people at practice on crumb rubber fields, and a follow-up biomonitoring study of 161 players, 132 on crumb rubber turf and 29 on grass, found similar before-and-after changes in urinary PAH levels for both groups.
quote: Personal air and dermal wipe samples were collected from 25 people participating in soccer or football practices at synthetic turf fields. … Among 161 participants, 82% (n=132) played on synthetic turf with tire crumb rubber infill, and the remaining 18% (n=29) played on natural grass. … Recycled tire crumb rubber infill field users and natural grass field users experienced similar differences in pre- and post-activity PAH concentrations
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary

fact: The federal report says neither part is a risk assessment and that the study was not designed, and is not sufficient by itself, to answer questions about health risks directly.
quote: Neither Part 1 nor Part 2 of this study, separately or combined, constitutes an assessment of the risks associated with playing on synthetic turf fields with recycled tire crumb rubber infill. … the study activities completed as part of this multi-agency research effort were not designed, and are not sufficient by themselves, to directly answer questions about potential health risks.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary

fact: The federal report quotes the Dutch RIVM, which called the health risk of playing on rubber-infilled fields virtually negligible, and the European Chemicals Agency, which found a very low level of concern and no reason to advise against playing on them.
quote: RIVM reported: “The results of this research indicate that playing sports on these fields is safe. The risk to health from playing sports on these synthetic turf fields is virtually negligible. While rubber granulate contains harmful substances, these substances are only released from the rubber granulate in very small quantities after ingestion, contact with the skin or evaporation in hot weather. …” … Conclusions from the ECHA reported: “ECHA has found no reason to advise people against playing sports on synthetic turf containing recycled rubber granules as infill material. This advice is based on ECHA’s evaluation that there is a very low level of concern from exposure to substances found in the granules.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary, citing RIVM (2017) and ECHA (2017)
notes: VERIFIED as what the federal report quotes; the RIVM and ECHA originals were not read (the ECHA site returned 403 to automated fetch). Attribute these to the federal report's quotation.

fact: The federal report quotes the National Toxicology Program: mice that ingested crumb rubber showed no toxicity, but in tests with human cells, crumb rubber under conditions such as high heat leached chemicals, some of which killed cells.
quote: Findings from the NTP research included: “There was no evidence of toxicity in mice from ingestion of crumb rubber. Analysis of the animals’ blood and urine showed that internal levels of crumb rubber chemicals were very low. No health problems were observed. For tests using human cells, NTP found that crumb rubber, under certain experimental conditions such as high heat, leached chemicals, some of which caused cell death.
source_label: U.S. EPA and CDC/ATSDR, Final Report Part 2: Exposure Characterization, Volume 1 (April 16, 2024), Executive Summary, citing NTP (2019)
notes: VERIFIED as the federal report's quotation of NTP; the NTP original was not read.

fact: EPA says tire crumb rubber is made by grinding scrap tires down to size and removing 99 percent or more of their steel and fabric.
quote: Tire crumb rubber is manufactured by reducing scrap tires down to various sizes depending on its intended application and market use, and by removing 99 percent or more of the steel and fabric from them.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Tire Crumb Questions and Answers (last updated March 10, 2026)

fact: The federal researchers took tire crumb samples from 40 playing fields across the four US census regions, indoor and outdoor, and from nine tire recycling plants, and ran the exposure studies at three of those fields.
quote: Tire crumb rubber samples were collected from 40 different playing fields within the four US census regions. These locations include both outdoor and indoor playing fields. The exposure pilot study and the supplemental biomonitoring study were conducted at three of these 40 fields. Samples were also collected from nine tire recycling facilities.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Tire Crumb Questions and Answers (last updated March 10, 2026)

fact: EPA says the tire crumb study did not test for specific PFAS, found no PFAS chemical in its broader screening of tire crumb rubber, and plans no further PFAS work on rubber or other turf parts.
quote: The tire crumb study did not specifically test for the presence of any PFAS target analytes.  No PFAS chemical was identified in the non-targeted analyses of tire crumb rubber.  No additional PFAS characterization of rubber or other turf components is planned.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Tire Crumb Questions and Answers (last updated March 10, 2026)

fact: EPA says 6PPD and 6PPD-quinone were not among the chemicals the federal study set out to measure, though 6PPD was tentatively identified in tire crumb samples from recycling plants and fields.
quote: Neither 6PPD nor 6PPD-quinone were target analytes in the FRAP research study. 6PPD was included as a suspect screening compound in the study and was tentatively identified in tire crumb rubber samples from tire recycling plants and in tire crumb rubber infill samples.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Tire Crumb Questions and Answers (last updated March 10, 2026)

fact: EPA says the Consumer Product Safety Commission will continue its playground work with a risk assessment of children's exposure to playground surfaces made of tire rubber, which had not been released when EPA last updated its page.
quote: CPSC will continue its work on playgrounds by conducting a risk assessment of children’s exposure to playground surfaces made of tire rubber.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Tire Crumb Questions and Answers (last updated March 10, 2026)
notes: The CPSC's own crumb rubber page returned 403 to automated fetch; re-check it in a browser and on EPA's page for a released playground risk assessment.

fact: Washington's Department of Health and the University of Washington, looking into a soccer coach's list of players with cancer that began with goalies who developed blood cancers, found less cancer among them than expected for Washington residents of the same ages and no increased cancer rate among the state's soccer players, though the investigation was not designed to test whether crumb rubber raises players' cancer risk.
quote: In 2009, the University of Washington Women's Associate Head Soccer Coach, Amy Griffin, became concerned that several soccer goalies had developed blood cancers at around the same time. … By 2016, the number on the coach's list had grown to 53 people. … In summary, the investigation found less cancer among the soccer players on coach Griffin’s list than expected cancer rates among Washington residents of the same ages. They did not find increased cancer rates among soccer players in Washington. Assurances of the safety of artificial turf with crumb rubber are limited by the lack of adequate information on potential toxicity and exposure. Note: The investigation was not designed to determine if soccer players in general were at increased risk of cancer due to exposures from crumb rubber in artificial turf.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Investigation of Reported Cancer Among Soccer Players in Washington State (DOH Pub 210-091, revised April 2017)

fact: Washington's Department of Health tells parents to be aware but not concerned: crumb rubber comes from tires containing chemicals shown to cause cancer, but the available research suggests exposures are very low, and it recommends that people keep playing soccer whatever the field surface.
quote: Parents should be aware, but not concerned. We know that crumb rubber is made from tires that contain chemicals that have been shown to cause cancer. However, what is critical to consider are the routes of exposure and potential dose someone receives. The available research suggests exposures from crumb rubber are very low and will not cause cancer among soccer players. The Washington State Department of Health recommends that people who enjoy soccer continue to play regardless of the type of field surface.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Investigation of Reported Cancer Among Soccer Players in Washington State: Frequently Asked Questions

fact: Washington's Department of Health lists ways to limit exposure to crumb rubber chemicals: wash hands after play and before eating, don't eat or drink on the turf, take off shoes, gear and dirty uniforms outside, clear crumbs from children's clothes, and spit out any pellets that get into the mouth.
quote: While available research does not show a significant health risk, there are several ways to minimize potential exposures to chemicals from artificial turf fields. Always wash hands after playing on the field and before eating. Avoid eating and drinking on turf surfaces. Take off shoes/cleats, sports equipment and soiled uniforms outside or in the garage to prevent tracking crumb rubber into homes. Remove crumb rubber traces from children’s clothing to prevent children from handling the crumb rubber themselves. Users of turf fields, especially children, should spit out any turf or infill pieces that get into the mouth, to avoid swallowing these materials.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf: How to limit exposure to chemicals in crumb rubber

fact: Washington's Department of Health says artificial turf managers should regularly monitor surface temperatures on hot days and set guidelines for when to warn users off the field.
quote: On hotter days, artificial turf managers should regularly monitor surface level temperatures and set guidelines for when to alert users to avoid field use.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf: Actions & Recommendations

fact: Washington's Department of Health notes that TURI's alternatives assessment found only organically managed natural grass to be a safer alternative to tire crumb infill, and that plant-based infills had the fewest chemicals of concern in some studies but can bring mold, allergen and fiber-inhalation hazards.
quote: Based on their alternatives assessment, TURI has only identified organically managed natural grass as a safer alternative to tire crumb rubber infill. Some studies that reviewed alternative infills couldn't identify any that are without health or environmental concerns. For example, some studies concluded that plant-based alternatives were found to contain the fewest chemicals of concern but could pose other hazards related to mold, allergens, and inhalation of fibers.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf: Safer alternatives to artificial turf

fact: Washington's Department of Health says tire crumb rubber has been found to contain 6PPD, 7PPD and 6PPD-quinone, whose hazards are an area of active research.
quote: Due to the use of 6PPD in tires, tire crumb rubber has also been found to contain 6PPD, 7PPD, and 6PPD-quinone. The hazards of these chemicals are an area of active research.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf: What are artificial turf fields made of?

fact: Since 10 August 2022, EU law bars selling or using rubber or other polymer granules or mulches, recycled or new, as infill on synthetic turf pitches or loose on playgrounds if they contain more than 20 mg/kg of eight listed PAHs combined; infill already in place on 9 August 2022 may stay.
quote: Granules or mulches shall not be placed on the market for use as infill material in synthetic turf pitches or in loose form on playgrounds or in sport applications if they contain more than 20 mg/kg (0,002 % by weight) of the sum of all listed PAHs. … Granules or mulches that are in use in the Union on 9 August 2022 as infill material in synthetic turf pitches or in loose form on playgrounds or in sport applications may remain in place and continue to be used there for the same purpose. … (a) “granules” are mixtures that appear as solid particles in the size range from 1 to 4 mm, which are made from rubber or other vulcanised or polymeric material of recycled or virgin origin, or obtained from a natural source;
source_label: Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1199 of 20 July 2021, amending REACH Annex XVII entry 50 (PAHs in granules or mulches), paragraphs 9 to 13
notes: Paragraph 12 sets the date: 'Paragraphs 9 to 11 shall apply from 10 August 2022.' The granules definition is paragraph 14(a).

fact: The EU set its PAH limit for infill because the eight PAHs are carcinogens for which no dose without a theoretical cancer risk can be derived, while its risk assessment committee said the 20 mg/kg figure is not based on estimated risk but aims to avoid very high PAH concentrations.
quote: The human health endpoint of utmost concern for these eight PAHs is carcinogenicity and the ability to induce genotoxic effects. For non-threshold carcinogens, a dose without a theoretical cancer risk cannot be derived. … RAC reiterated that the proposed 20 mg/kg limit is not based upon the estimated risk but it is a measure aimed solely at avoiding very high PAH concentrations.
source_label: Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1199 of 20 July 2021, recitals

fact: The EU's microplastics restriction bars placing synthetic polymer microparticles on the market as granular infill for synthetic sports surfaces from 17 October 2031, an 8-year transition meant to let more existing fields reach the end of their life first.
quote: (j) from 17 October 2031 for granular infill for use on synthetic sports surfaces. … For granular infill for use on synthetic sports surfaces, the Commission considers that increasing the transitional period for the ban on placing on the market to 8 years is justified in order to ensure that a larger number of existing synthetic sport surfaces using this product can reach their natural end-of-life before they need to be replaced.
source_label: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/2055 of 25 September 2023 (REACH Annex XVII entry 78, synthetic polymer microparticles), paragraph 6(j) and recital 53
notes: Environmental shedding belongs to artificial-turf-microplastics; this page mentions the date once and links there.
